title: Pelacarsen and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients with High Lipoprotein(a)
abstract: BACKGROUND: Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] is an independent, genetically determined risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, but it was unknown whether pharmacologic lowering of Lp(a) reduces cardiovascular events. Pelacarsen is an antisense oligonucleotide directed at hepatic apolipoprotein(a) synthesis. Lp(a)HORIZON (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04023552) was designed to test the Lp(a) hypothesis in secondary prevention. METHODS: Lp(a)HORIZON was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multinational trial conducted at 797 sites in 42 countries. Eligible patients had established cardiovascular disease, with a qualifying cardiovascular event between 3 months and 10 years before enrollment, and a baseline Lp(a) level of at least 70 mg/dL (approximately 148 nmol/L). Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to pelacarsen 80 mg administered subcutaneously once monthly or to matching placebo administered on the same schedule, on a background of guideline-directed therapy. Randomization was stratified by screening Lp(a) level so as to balance patients with Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL (approximately 192 nmol/L), who constituted a prespecified second primary analysis population. The primary endpoint was expanded major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE): a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, and urgent coronary revascularization. A total of 8,350 patients were randomly assigned and 8,322 were included in the efficacy analysis. RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 4.7 years, the primary expanded-MACE endpoint occurred in 12.3% of patients assigned to pelacarsen and in 12.1% of patients assigned to placebo (hazard ratio, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.90 to 1.15). The exact P value for the primary comparison could not be verified in the available secondary sources and is therefore not reported here. The neutral result was consistent across the individual components of the composite. In the prespecified population with baseline Lp(a) of at least 90 mg/dL, the primary endpoint occurred in 12.3% of patients in each group (hazard ratio, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.15). Pelacarsen had the expected biologic effect on its target: Lp(a) was reduced by 78.4% at 12 months, with a median Lp(a) at 12 months of 64.4 nmol/L with pelacarsen versus 233.4 nmol/L with placebo. Reported safety and tolerability details beyond the above (including rates of study-drug discontinuation, which were reported as higher with pelacarsen) could not be confirmed by two independent sources and are not reported here. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with established cardiovascular disease and an Lp(a) level of at least 70 mg/dL, pelacarsen 80 mg subcutaneously once monthly lowered Lp(a) by approximately 78% but did not reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events as compared with placebo over a median of 4.7 years. The investigators have stated that the findings were unexpected and disappointing and that they apply specifically to pelacarsen in a secondary-prevention setting, rather than invalidating Lp(a) as a causal risk factor.

title: Interleukin-6 Inhibition with Ziltivekimab for Atherosclerotic Disease
abstract: BACKGROUND: Residual inflammatory risk, marked by elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hs-CRP), persists in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) despite lipid-lowering therapy. Ziltivekimab is a fully human monoclonal antibody directed against the interleukin-6 (IL-6) ligand. The ZEUS trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05021835) tested whether IL-6 inhibition reduces cardiovascular events in patients with ASCVD, chronic kidney disease (CKD) and systemic inflammation. METHODS: ZEUS was a multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, event-driven trial. Eligible patients had established ASCVD together with CKD and an hs-CRP level of at least 2 mg/L. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to ziltivekimab 15 mg administered subcutaneously once monthly or to matching placebo. The primary endpoint was the time to first occurrence of 3-point MACE, a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction and nonfatal stroke. The full analysis population comprised 6,376 patients: 3,184 assigned to ziltivekimab and 3,192 assigned to placebo. Median baseline hs-CRP was 4.5 mg/L. RESULTS: Over a median follow-up of 33 months, the primary 3-point MACE endpoint occurred in 17.6% of patients assigned to ziltivekimab and in 17.7% of patients assigned to placebo (hazard ratio, 0.99; 95% CI, 0.88 to 1.11; P=0.84). All-cause mortality did not differ between groups. Ziltivekimab engaged its target as expected: at 24 months the between-group difference in median percent change in hs-CRP was approximately -64 percentage points, and IL-6 was likewise markedly reduced. Overall rates of adverse events and of serious adverse events were similar between the two groups (54.6% with ziltivekimab vs 54.8% with placebo). Serious infections were more frequent with ziltivekimab than with placebo (20.4% vs 17.9%), as were deaths attributed to infection (3.2% vs 2.5%) and serious venous thromboembolism (1.6% vs 0.6%). CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease and an hs-CRP level of at least 2 mg/L, once-monthly subcutaneous ziltivekimab 15 mg produced large reductions in IL-6 and hs-CRP but did not reduce the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events as compared with placebo, and was associated with an excess of serious infections. The investigators and commentators have emphasized that the neutral result does not in itself refute the inflammatory hypothesis of atherosclerosis.

title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Control in Patients with Previous Ischemic Stroke
abstract: BACKGROUND: The optimal systolic blood-pressure (SBP) target for secondary prevention after ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA) is uncertain, and previous trials have not established whether a target below 120 mm Hg is superior to the conventional target below 140 mm Hg in this population. OPTIMAL-STROKE (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04036409) was designed to address this question. METHODS: OPTIMAL-STROKE was an investigator-initiated, multicenter, randomized, open-label trial with blinded endpoint adjudication by a clinical events committee, conducted at 30 sites in Brazil, with enrollment from August 2019 through August 2022. Eligible patients had a previous ischemic stroke or TIA, were clinically stable for at least 48 hours, and had elevated SBP (reported as a range of 130 to 180 mm Hg). Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to intensive treatment targeting an SBP of less than 120 mm Hg or to standard treatment targeting an SBP of less than 140 mm Hg, using open-label antihypertensive therapy. The primary outcome was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure. A total of 4,368 patients were randomly assigned: 2,172 to intensive treatment and 2,196 to standard treatment. RESULTS: Mean SBP after the first 3 months was 122.0 mm Hg in the intensive-treatment group and 135.2 mm Hg in the standard-treatment group, a between-group separation of approximately 13 mm Hg. Over a median follow-up of 3.9 years, the primary composite outcome occurred in 236 patients (10.9%) in the intensive-treatment group and in 297 patients (13.5%) in the standard-treatment group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% CI, 0.67 to 0.94; P=0.007). This corresponds to an absolute between-group difference of 2.6 percentage points and a relative risk reduction of approximately 21%. With respect to safety, rates of serious adverse events, orthostatic hypotension and injuries were similar in the two groups, whereas renal events were more frequent with intensive treatment, a finding the investigators attributed mainly to a hemodynamic reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with previous ischemic stroke or TIA and elevated blood pressure, targeting an SBP of less than 120 mm Hg reduced the incidence of major cardiovascular events as compared with a target of less than 140 mm Hg. The investigators call for individualized treatment and careful monitoring of renal function, given the excess of renal events in the intensive-treatment group. The American Heart Association describes the findings as preliminary until peer-reviewed publication is fully disseminated.

title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Lowering in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes
abstract: BACKGROUND: Whether a systolic blood-pressure (SBP) target below 120 mm Hg reduces cardiovascular events in patients with type 2 diabetes remains contested: ACCORD-BP was neutral whereas the more recent BPROAD trial in China was positive. OPTIMAL-DIABETES (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04040634) was designed to test an intensive target in an ethnically diverse, high-cardiovascular-risk diabetic population. METHODS: OPTIMAL-DIABETES was a multicenter, randomized, open-label trial conducted in Brazil. Eligible patients were adults (reported as 50 years of age or older) with elevated blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk, defined by established cardiovascular disease, subclinical cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease or other cardiovascular risk factors. Patients were randomly assigned to intensive therapy targeting an SBP of less than 120 mm Hg or to standard therapy targeting an SBP of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary outcome was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure. Of 9,476 patients enrolled, 4,745 were assigned to intensive therapy and 4,731 to standard therapy. RESULTS: Mean SBP during follow-up was approximately 122 mm Hg in the intensive-therapy group and approximately 135 mm Hg in the standard-therapy group. Over a median follow-up of 4.0 years, the primary composite outcome occurred in 6.0% of patients in the intensive-therapy group and in 6.7% of patients in the standard-therapy group (hazard ratio, 0.90; P=0.20); the 95% confidence interval for this hazard ratio could not be confirmed by two independent sources and is therefore not reported here. The difference was not statistically significant. Rates of serious adverse events were similar in the two groups. Renal events were reported to be more frequent with intensive therapy, attributed mainly to a hemodynamic reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate, although this was corroborated by only one source. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with type 2 diabetes, elevated blood pressure and high cardiovascular risk, targeting an SBP of less than 120 mm Hg did not reduce the incidence of major cardiovascular events as compared with a target of less than 140 mm Hg. The investigators explicitly caution that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that more intensive blood-pressure lowering is ineffective in people with type 2 diabetes: they suggest that any cardiovascular benefit may be smaller in diabetes than in people without diabetes, such that a trial of this size may not have been able to detect a modest yet clinically meaningful effect.
